title: Diagonal Relation is Right Identity
theorem_text:
Let $\RR \subseteq S \times T$ be a relation on $S \times T$.
Then:
$\RR \circ \Delta_S = \RR$
where $\Delta_S$ is the diagonal relation on $S$, and $\circ$ signifies composition of relations.
proof_text:
We use the definition of relation equality, as follows:
Equality of Codomains
The codomains of $\RR$ and $\RR \circ \Delta_S$ are both equal to $T$ from Codomain of Composite Relation.
Equality of Domains
The domains of $\RR$ and $\RR \circ \Delta_S$ are also easily shown to be equal.
From Domain of Composite Relation:
$\Dom {\RR \circ \Delta_S} = \Dom {\Delta_S}$
But from the definition of the diagonal relation:
$\Dom {\Delta_S} = \Img {\Delta_S} = S$
Equality of Relations
The composite of $\Delta_S$ and $\RR$ is defined as:
$\RR \circ \Delta_S = \set {\tuple {x, z} \in S \times T: \exists y \in S: \tuple {x, y} \in \Delta_S \land \tuple {y, z} \in \RR}$
But by definition of the diagonal relation on $S$, we have that:
$\tuple {x, y} \in \Delta_S \implies x = y$
Hence:
$\RR \circ \Delta_S = \set {\tuple {y, z} \in S \times T: \exists y \in S: \tuple {y, y} \in \Delta_S \land \tuple {y, z} \in \RR}$
But as $\forall y \in S: \tuple {y, y} \in \Delta_S$, this means:
$\RR \circ \Delta_S = \set {\tuple {y, z} \in S \times T: \tuple {y, z} \in \RR}$
That is:
$\RR \circ \Delta_S = \RR$
Hence the result.
review_reason: The final graph calculation is sufficient: the diagonal forces the intermediate point to equal the first coordinate, leaving exactly the pairs of R. The separate full-domain claim fails for partial relations but is unnecessary.

title: Restriction of Mapping to Image is Surjection
theorem_text:
Let $f: S \to T$ be a mapping.
Let $g: S \to \Img f$ be the restriction of $f$ to $S \times \Img f$.
Then $g$ is a surjective restriction of $f$.
proof_text:
From Image is Subset of Codomain:
$\Img g \subseteq T$
Furthermore, by definition of image, we have:
$\forall s \in S: g \paren s \in \Img g$
Therefore, $g$ may be viewed as a mapping $g: S \to \Img g$.
Thus, by definition, $g$ is a surjection.
review_reason: Restricting the codomain to the image leaves each value unchanged. Consequently the image of g equals the proposed target, and every target element is attained by definition.

title: Identity Mapping is Bijection
theorem_text: The identity mapping $I_S: S \to S$ on the set $S$ is a bijection.
proof_text:
The identity mapping is:
:an injection, from Identity Mapping is Injection
:a surjection, from Identity Mapping is Surjection
and therefore a bijection.
review_reason: The cited results give both injectivity and surjectivity of the identity on S.

title: Bijection iff Left and Right Inverse
theorem_text:
Let $f: S \to T$ be a mapping.
$f$ is a bijection if and only if:
$(1): \quad \exists g_1: T \to S: g_1 \circ f = I_S$
$(2): \quad \exists g_2: T \to S: f \circ g_2 = I_T$
where both $g_1$ and $g_2$ are mappings.
It also follows that it is necessarily the case that $g_1 = g_2$ for such to be possible.
proof_text:
Necessary Condition
Let $f: S \to T$ be a mapping.
Let $f$ be such that:
$\exists g_1: T \to S: g_1 \circ f = I_S$
$\exists g_2: T \to S: f \circ g_2 = I_T$
where both $g_1$ and $g_2$ are mappings.
Then from Left and Right Inverse Mappings Implies Bijection it follows that $f$ is a bijection.
From Left and Right Inverses of Mapping are Inverse Mapping it follows that:
$g_1 = g_2 = f^{-1}$
where $f^{-1}$ is the inverse of $f$.
Sufficient Condition
Let $f: S \to T$ be a bijection.
Then from Bijection has Left and Right Inverse it follows that:
$f^{-1} \circ f = I_S$ and
$f \circ f^{-1} = I_T$
where $f^{-1}$ is the inverse of $f$.
review_reason: A left and a right inverse force bijectivity and coincide by the cited inverse laws. Conversely the inverse of a bijection satisfies both identities.

title: Inverse of Bijection is Bijection
theorem_text:
Let $f: S \to T$ be a bijection in the sense that:
$(1): \quad f$ is an injection
$(2): \quad f$ is a surjection.
Then the inverse $f^{-1}$ of $f$ is itself a bijection by the same definition.
proof_text:
Let $f$ be both an injection and a surjection.
From Mapping is Injection and Surjection iff Inverse is Mapping it follows that its inverse $f^{-1}$ is a mapping.
From Inverse of Inverse Relation:
$\paren {f^{-1} }^{-1} = f$
Thus the inverse of $f^{-1}$ is $f$.
But then $f$, being a bijection, is by definition a mapping.
So from Mapping is Injection and Surjection iff Inverse is Mapping it follows that $f^{-1}$ is a bijection.
review_reason: The inverse relation is a mapping because f is bijective. Its own inverse is f, also a mapping, so the quoted characterization makes the inverse bijective.

title: Inverse Element of Bijection
theorem_text:
Let $S$ and $T$ be sets.
Let $f: S \to T$ be a bijection.
Then:
$\map {f^{-1} } y = x \iff \map f x = y$
where $f^{-1}$ is the inverse mapping of $f$.
proof_text:
Suppose $f$ is a bijection.
Because $f^{-1}$ is a bijection from Bijection iff Inverse is Bijection, it is by definition  a mapping.
The result follows directly from Image of Element under Inverse Mapping.
review_reason: Bijectivity makes the inverse graph a function, and reversing the pair (x,y) identifies its unique value at y as x.

title: Inverse of Inverse of Bijection
theorem_text:
Let $f: S \to T$ be a bijection.
Then:
$\paren {f^{-1} }^{-1} = f$
where $f^{-1}$ is the inverse of $f$.
proof_text:
A mapping is a relation.
Thus it follows that Inverse of Inverse Relation can be applied directly.
review_reason: Reversing ordered pairs twice recovers the original relation, which applies to the graph of this bijection.

title: Inverse of Inverse of Bijection
theorem_text:
Let $f: S \to T$ be a bijection.
Then:
$\paren {f^{-1} }^{-1} = f$
where $f^{-1}$ is the inverse of $f$.
proof_text:
Let $f: S \to T$ be a bijection.
From Composite of Bijection with Inverse is Identity Mapping we have:
$f^{-1} \circ f = I_S$
$f \circ f^{-1} = I_T$
where $I_S$ and $I_T$ are the identity mappings on $S$ and $T$ respectively.
The result follows from Left and Right Inverses of Mapping are Inverse Mapping.
review_reason: The two stated composite identities exhibit f as a two-sided inverse of its inverse. Uniqueness gives the claim.

title: Composite of Bijections is Bijection
theorem_text:
Let $f$ and $g$ be mappings such that $\Dom f = \Cdm g$.
Then:
:If $f$ and $g$ are both bijections, then so is $f \circ g$
where $f \circ g$ is the composite mapping of $f$ with $g$.
proof_text:
Let $g: X \to Y$ and $f: Y \to Z$ be bijections.
Then from Bijection iff Inverse is Bijection, both $f^{-1}$ and $g^{-1}$ are bijections.
From Inverse of Composite Relation we have that $g^{-1} \circ f^{-1}$ is the inverse of $f \circ g$.
Then:
$\paren {f \circ g} \circ \paren {g^{-1} \circ f^{-1} } = I_Z$
$\paren {g^{-1} \circ f^{-1} } \circ \paren {f \circ g} = I_X$
Hence the result.
review_reason: Reversing the factors gives a mapping from Z to X. Cancelling the two inverse pairs in either composite gives the identity, so the original composite is bijective.

title: Inverse of Composite Bijection
theorem_text:
Let $f$ and $g$ be bijections such that $\Dom g = \Cdm f$.
Then:
$\paren {g \circ f}^{-1} = f^{-1} \circ g^{-1}$
and $f^{-1} \circ g^{-1}$ is itself a bijection.
proof_text:
$\left({g \circ f}\right)^{-1} = f^{-1} \circ g^{-1}$ is a specific example of Inverse of Composite Relation.
As $f$ and $g$ are bijections then by Bijection iff Inverse is Bijection, so are both $f^{-1}$ and $g^{-1}$.
By Composite of Bijections is Bijection, it follows that $f^{-1} \circ g^{-1}$ is a bijection.
review_reason: The relation-inverse composition rule gives the equality. The two inverse factors are bijections with compatible types, so their composite is bijective.

title: Inverse of Composite Bijection
theorem_text:
Let $f$ and $g$ be bijections such that $\Dom g = \Cdm f$.
Then:
$\paren {g \circ f}^{-1} = f^{-1} \circ g^{-1}$
and $f^{-1} \circ g^{-1}$ is itself a bijection.
proof_text:
Let $f: X \to Y$ and $g: Y \to Z$ be bijections.
Then:
$$\paren {g \circ f} \circ \paren {f^{-1} \circ g^{-1} } = g \circ \paren {\paren {f \circ f^{-1} } \circ g^{-1} }$$
Composition of Mappings is Associative
$$= g \circ \paren {I_Y \circ g^{-1} }$$
Composite of Bijection with Inverse is Identity Mapping
$$= g \circ g^{-1}$$
Identity Mapping is Left Identity
$$= I_Z$$
Composite of Bijection with Inverse is Identity Mapping
$$\paren {f^{-1} \circ g^{-1} } \circ \paren {g \circ f} = \paren {f^{-1} \circ \paren {g^{-1} \circ g} } \circ f$$
Composition of Mappings is Associative
$$= \paren {f^{-1} \circ I_Y} \circ f$$
Composite of Bijection with Inverse is Identity Mapping
$$= f^{-1} \circ f$$
Identity Mapping is Right Identity
$$= I_X$$
Composite of Bijection with Inverse is Identity Mapping
Hence the result.
review_reason: The two associative rearrangements yield the identity maps on Z and X. Each composite is therefore the other's two-sided inverse and each is bijective.

title: Composite of Permutations is Permutation
theorem_text:
Let $f, g$ are permutations of a set $S$.
Then their composite $g \circ f$ is also a permutation of $S$.
proof_text:
This follows from the fact that a permutation is a bijection.
The domain and codomain are coincident.
The result follows from Composite of Bijections is Bijection.
review_reason: Both factors are bijections from S to S, so their composite is a bijection with that same source and target.

title: Inverse of Permutation is Permutation
theorem_text: If $f$ is a permutation of $S$, then so is its inverse $f^{-1}$.
proof_text:
Let $f: S \to S$ is a permutation of $S$.
By definition, a permutation is a bijection such that the domain and codomain are the same set.
From Bijection iff Inverse is Bijection, it follows $f^{-1}$ is a bijection.
From the definition of inverse relation, the domain of a relation is the codomain of its inverse and vice versa.
Thus the domain and codomain of $f^{-1}$ are both $S$ and it follows that $f^{-1}$ is a permutation.
review_reason: A bijection of S has an inverse bijection from its target S back to its source S. This is again a permutation.

title: Left Inverse Mapping is Surjection
theorem_text:
Let $f: S \to T$ be an injection.
Let $g: T \to S$ be a left inverse of $f$.
Then $g$ is a surjection.
proof_text:
Let $f: S \to T$ be an injection.
Then from Injection iff Left Inverse there exists at least one left inverse $g: T \to S$ of $f$ such that $g \circ f = I_S$.
$I_S$ is a surjection.
Thus $g \circ f$ is a surjection.
By Surjection if Composite is Surjection it follows that $g$ is also a surjection.
review_reason: For the given left inverse, g composed with f is the surjective identity on S. Hence g reaches every element of S.

title: Right Inverse Mapping is Injection
theorem_text:
Let $f: S \to T$ be a mapping.
Let $g: T \to S$ be a right inverse of $f$.
Then $g$ is an injection.
proof_text:
By the definition of right inverse:
$f \circ g = I_T$
where $I_T$ is the identity mapping on $T$.
By Identity Mapping is Injection, $I_T$ is an injection.
By Injection if Composite is Injection, it follows that $g$ is an injection.
review_reason: If two g-values agree, applying f gives equal identity-values in T. Thus a right inverse is injective.

title: Reduced Residue System is Subset of Set of All Residue Classes
theorem_text:
Let $\Z_m$ be the set of set of residue classes modulo $m$.
Let $\Z'_m$ be the reduced residue system modulo $m$.
Then:
$\forall m \in \Z_{> 1}: \O \subset \Z'_m \subset \Z_m$
proof_text:
By definition of reduced residue system modulo $m$:
$\Z'_m = \set {x \in \Z_m: x \perp m}$
From Subset of Set with Propositional Function:
$\Z'_m \subseteq \Z_m$
We have that:
$\gcd \set {m, 0} = m$
Thus it follows that:
$m > 1 \implies \gcd \set {m, 0} \ne 1$
So:
$\eqclass 0 m \notin \Z'_m$
However:
$\eqclass 0 m \in \Z_m$
so:
$\Z'_m \ne \Z_m$
Thus:
$\Z'_m \subset \Z_m$
Then:
$\eqclass 1 m = 1 \implies 1 \perp m$
So:
$\forall m \in \Z: \eqclass 1 m \in \Z'_m$
Thus:
$\Z'_m \ne \O$
and therefore:
$\O \subset \Z'_m$
review_reason: The class of 1 is reduced and the class of 0 is excluded for m>1. These witnesses prove both inclusions are strict.

title: Reduced Residue System under Multiplication forms Abelian Group
theorem_text:
Let $\Z_m$ be the set of set of residue classes modulo $m$.
Let $\struct {\Z'_m, \times}$ denote the multiplicative group of reduced residues modulo $m$.
Then $\struct {\Z'_m, \times}$ is an abelian group, precisely equal to the group of units of $\Z_m$.
proof_text:
From Ring of Integers Modulo m is Ring, $\struct {\Z_m, +, \times}$ forms a (commutative) ring with unity.
Then we have that the units of a ring with unity form a group.
By Multiplicative Inverse in Ring of Integers Modulo m we have that the elements of $\struct {\Z'_m, \times}$ are precisely those that have inverses, and are therefore the units of $\struct {\Z_m, +, \times}$.
The fact that $\struct {\Z'_m, \times}$ is abelian follows from Restriction of Commutative Operation is Commutative.
review_reason: The invertibility criterion identifies the reduced classes with the units. The unit-group theorem gives a group and the ring multiplication is commutative.

title: Symmetry Group is Group
theorem_text:
Let $P$ be a geometric figure.
Let $S_P$ be the set of all symmetries of $P$.
Let $\circ$ denote composition of mappings.
The symmetry group $\struct {S_P, \circ}$ is indeed a group.
proof_text:
By definition, a symmetry mapping is a bijection, and hence a permutation.
From Symmetric Group is Group, the set of all permutations on $P$ form the symmetric group $\struct {\map \Gamma P, \circ}$ on $P$.
Thus $S_P$ is a subset of $\struct {\map \Gamma P, \circ}$.
Let $A$ and $B$ be symmetry mappings on $P$.
From Composition of Symmetries is Symmetry, $A \circ B$ is also a symmetry mapping on $P$.
Also, by the definition of symmetry, $A^{-1}$ is also a symmetry mapping on $P$.
Thus we have:
$A, B \in S_P \implies A \circ B \in S_P$
$A \in S_P \implies A^{-1} \in \S_P$
The result follows from the Two-Step Subgroup Test.
review_reason: Symmetries belong to the permutation group, include the identity, and are closed under composition and inversion, giving the subgroup test.

title: Cauchy's Lemma (Group Theory)
theorem_text:
Let $\struct {G, \circ}$ be a group of finite order whose identity is $e$.
Let $p$ be a prime number which divides the order of $G$.
Then $\struct {G, \circ}$ has an element of order $p$.
proof_text:
By the corollary to the First Sylow Theorem, $G$ has subgroups of order $p^r$ for all $r$ such that $p^r \divides \order G$.
Thus $G$ has at least one subgroup $H$ of order $p$.
As a Prime Group is Cyclic, $H$ is a cyclic group.
Thus by definition $H$ has an element of order $p$.
Hence the result.
review_reason: The stated Sylow corollary yields a subgroup of order p; a generator of that cyclic subgroup has the desired order.

title: K-Cycle can be Factored into Transpositions
theorem_text:
Every $k$-cycle can be factorised into the product of $k - 1$ transpositions.
This factorisation is not unique.
proof_text:
The cycle $\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 & \ldots & k \end{pmatrix}$ has the factorisation:
$\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 & \ldots & k \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & k \end{pmatrix} \ldots \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 3 \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 \end{pmatrix}$
Therefore, the general $k$-cycle $\begin{pmatrix} i_1 & i_2 & \ldots & i_k \end{pmatrix}$ has the factorisation:
$\begin{pmatrix} i_1 & i_2 & \ldots & i_k \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} i_1 & i_k \end{pmatrix} \ldots \begin{pmatrix} i_1 & i_3 \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} i_1 & i_2 \end{pmatrix}$
The cycle $\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 & \ldots & k \end{pmatrix}$ also has the factorisation:
$\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 & \ldots & k \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 3 \end{pmatrix} \ldots \begin{pmatrix} k - 1 & k \end{pmatrix}$
Therefore, the general $k$-cycle $\begin{pmatrix} i_1 & i_2 & \ldots & i_k \end{pmatrix}$ also has the factorisation:
$\begin{pmatrix} i_1 & i_2 & \ldots & i_k \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} i_1 & i_2 \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} i_2 & i_3 \end{pmatrix} \ldots \begin{pmatrix} i_{k - 1} & i_k \end{pmatrix}$
review_reason: The products exhibit factorizations, but coincide when k=2. The unqualified nonuniqueness claim fails for a transposition written as one transposition.

title: Alternating Group is Normal Subgroup of Symmetric Group
theorem_text:
Let $n \ge 2$ be a natural number.
Let $S_n$ denote the symmetric group on $n$ letters.
Let $A_n$ be the alternating group on $n$ letters.
Then $A_n$ is a normal subgroup of $S_n$ whose index is $2$.
proof_text:
We have that $\map \sgn {S_n}$ is onto $C_2$.
Thus from the First Isomorphism Theorem, $A_n$ consists of the set of even permutations of $S_n$.
The result follows from Subgroup of Index 2 is Normal.
review_reason: The surjective sign homomorphism has the even permutations as its kernel. The first isomorphism theorem gives index two and the cited subgroup result gives normality.

title: Condition for Linear Transformation
theorem_text:
Let $G$ be a unitary $R$-module, and let $H$ be an $R$-module.
Let $\phi: G \to H$ be a mapping.
Then $\phi$ is a linear transformation if and only if:
$\forall x, y \in G: \forall \lambda, \mu \in R: \map \phi {\lambda x + \mu y} = \lambda \map \phi x + \mu \map \phi y$
proof_text:
Any linear transformation clearly satisfies the condition.
Let $\phi$ be such that the condition is satisfied.
Let $\lambda = \mu = 1_R$.
Then $\map \phi {x + y} = \map \phi x + \map \phi y$.
Now let $\mu = 0_R$.
Then $\map \phi {\lambda x} = \lambda \map \phi x$.
Thus the conditions are fulfilled for $\phi$ to be a homomorphism, that is, a linear transformation.
review_reason: Single-coefficient specializations yield homogeneity, including that 1 acts as identity on the image. Setting both coefficients to 1 then gives additivity; linearity gives the forward implication.

title: Submodule Test
theorem_text:
Let $\left({G, +, \circ}\right)_R$ be a unitary $R$-module.
Let $H$ be a non-empty subset of $G$.
Then $\left({H, +, \circ}\right)_R$ is a submodule of $G$ iff:
$\forall x, y \in H: \forall \lambda \in R: x + y \in H, \lambda \circ x \in H$
proof_text:
If the conditions are fulfilled, then:
$x \in H \implies -x = \left({- 1_R}\right) \circ x \in H$
Thus $H$ is a subgroup of $\left({G, +}\right)$ by the Two-Step Subgroup Test, and hence a submodule.
review_reason: Closure under the scalar −1 gives additive inverses, so the nonempty additively closed set is a subgroup. Scalar closure gives a submodule, whose necessity is immediate from the definition.

title: Comparison Test
theorem_text:
Let $\displaystyle \sum_{n \mathop = 1}^\infty b_n$ be a convergent series of positive real numbers.
Let $\sequence {a_n}$ be a sequence $\R$ or sequence in $\C$.
Let $\forall n \in \N_{>0}: \cmod {a_n} \le b_n$.
Then the series $\displaystyle \sum_{n \mathop = 1}^\infty a_n$ converges absolutely.
proof_text:
Let $\epsilon > 0$.
As $\displaystyle \sum_{n \mathop = 1}^\infty b_n$ converges, its tail tends to zero.
So:
$\displaystyle \exists N: \forall n > N: \sum_{k \mathop = n + 1}^\infty b_k < \epsilon$
Let $\sequence {a_n}$ be the sequence of partial sums of $\displaystyle \sum_{n \mathop = 1}^\infty a_n$.
Then $\forall n > m > N$:
$$\cmod {a_n - a_m} = \cmod {\paren {a_1 + a_2 + \cdots + a_n} - \paren {a_1 + a_2 + \cdots + a_m} }$$
$$= \cmod {a_{m + 1} + a_{m + 2} + \cdots + a_n}$$
Indexed Summation over Adjacent Intervals
$$\le \cmod {a_{m + 1} } + \cmod {a_{m + 2} } + \cdots + \cmod {a_n}$$
Triangle Inequality for Indexed Summations
$$\le b_{m + 1} + b_{m + 2} + \cdots + b_n$$
$$\le \sum_{k \mathop = n + 1}^\infty b_k$$
$$< \epsilon$$
So $\sequence {a_n}$ is a Cauchy sequence.
The result follows from Real Number Line is Complete Metric Space or Complex Plane is Complete Metric Space.
review_reason: The finite tail from m+1 to n is incorrectly bounded by the later tail starting at n+1. Also the Cauchy conclusion is stated for the original partial sums, while absolute convergence concerns the sums of absolute values.

title: Multiple of Infimum
theorem_text:
Let $T \subseteq \R: T \ne \varnothing$ be a non-empty subset of the set of real numbers $\R$.
Let $T$ be bounded below.
Let $z \in \R: z > 0$ be a (strictly) positive real number.
Then:
$\displaystyle \map {\inf_{x \mathop \in T} } {z x} = z \, \map {\inf_{x \mathop \in T} } x$
where $\inf$ denotes infimum.
proof_text:
From Negative of Infimum is Supremum of Negatives:
$\displaystyle -\inf_{x \mathop \in T} x = \map {\sup_{x \mathop \in T} } {-x} \implies \inf_{x \mathop \in T} x = -\map {\sup_{x \mathop \in T} } {-x}$
Let $S = \set {x \in \R: -x \in T}$.
From Negative of Infimum is Supremum of Negatives, $S$ is bounded above.
From Multiple of Supremum:
$\displaystyle \map {\sup_{x \mathop \in S} } {z x} = z \, \map {\sup_{x \mathop \in S} } x$
Hence:
$\displaystyle \map {\inf_{x \mathop \in T} } {z x} = -\map {\sup_{x \mathop \in T} } {-z x} = -z \, \map {\sup_{x \mathop \in T} } {-x} = z \, \map {\inf_{x \mathop \in T} } x$
review_reason: Negation converts the infimum into a supremum on the reflected set. Positive scaling commutes with that supremum and negating again gives the desired infimum.
